astronomy/black-holes.4492b1e31acb: The Sun. A normal star: a gentle dip. The Sun is one point four million kilometers, eight hundred seventy thousand miles, wide and holds ninety-nine point eight percent of the Solar System’s mass. Its gravity curves spacetime gently: the planets roll around the dip in orbits. To escape from its surface you need six hundred eighteen kilometers per second, only zero point two percent of the speed of light. The Sun will never become a black hole: it isn’t massive enough. It will end as a white dwarf. Same mass, bigger size, gentler dip.
astronomy/black-holes.7ebd2f98770f: White dwarf, Sirius B. A Sun’s mass squeezed to Earth’s size. Sirius B has about the Sun’s mass packed into a ball smaller than Earth. A teaspoon of white-dwarf matter would weigh several tons on Earth. Escape speed from its surface: about six thousand eight hundred kilometers per second, a little over two percent of light speed. This is how stars like our Sun end their lives. Smaller ball, same mass, deeper dip near it.
astronomy/black-holes.9894c4344cde: Black hole, Cygnus X one. About twenty-one Suns inside a sixty-two-kilometer horizon. Cygnus X one was the first object widely accepted as a black hole, nineteen seventies. It is about seven thousand light-years away. Its event horizon has a radius of about sixty-two kilometers, thirty-nine miles. At the event horizon the escape speed equals the speed of light, so nothing inside can get out, not even light. We “see” it because gas pulled from its companion star heats up to millions of degrees and glows in X-rays. Event horizon equals the point of no return.
astronomy/black-holes.01ae12602951: Neutron star. One point four Suns squeezed to the size of a city. A neutron star is about twenty-four kilometers, fifteen miles, across, roughly the size of a city like Atlanta. It is made almost entirely of neutrons packed as tightly as in an atomic nucleus. Escape speed from its surface is about sixty percent of the speed of light. Squeezed inside a radius of about four kilometers, the same mass would be a black hole. Neutron star: one step away from a black hole.

astronomy/exoplanets.666f0d57e75b: Earth crossing the Sun. A tiny dip once a year. Earth is one hundred nine times narrower than the Sun, so it blocks only one over one hundred nine, all squared, about zero point zero zero eight four percent of the light: eighty-four parts per million. The transit lasts about thirteen hours, once every three hundred sixty-five days. Only a telescope in space, like Kepler, is steady enough to measure such a tiny dip. Turn on “Add noise” to see why small planets are hard to find. Earth-size planet and Sun-size star equals a dip smaller than the noise.
astronomy/exoplanets.a27bdf381608: Kepler four five two b. A “cousin” of Earth found by Kepler, twenty fifteen. About one point six times as wide as Earth, with a three hundred eighty-five-day year around a Sun-like star. About one thousand eight hundred light-years away, much too far to visit. Its dip is only about zero point zero two percent deep, so it took four years of Kepler data to find. We still don’t know if it is rocky or more like a small Neptune. Long year and small planet equals years of watching.
astronomy/exoplanets.7c96bcba2f3c: Common mix-up: A transit is not an eclipse that makes the star go dark. Even Jupiter blocks only about one percent of the Sun.
astronomy/exoplanets.b9a5c9c6a33f: TRAPPIST one e. An Earth-size planet around a tiny red star. TRAPPIST one is a red dwarf only a little bigger than Jupiter, about forty light-years away. Because the star is so small, an Earth-size planet blocks about zero point five percent of its light: sixty times more than Earth blocks of the Sun. Its year lasts just six point one days. The star has seven known rocky planets. TRAPPIST one e sits in the star’s habitable zone, see below. Small star, deeper dip for the same planet.
astronomy/exoplanets.ae12599d47dc: Jupiter crossing the Sun. What aliens would see. Seen from far away, Jupiter would dim the Sun by about one percent. But it transits only once every eleven point nine years, and each transit lasts about thirty hours. To confirm it, an alien astronomer would need to watch for decades! That is why most planets found so far have short years: they are much easier to catch. Long year, rare transits, hard to find.
astronomy/exoplanets.42c24a0e5b74: Hot Jupiter: HD two zero nine four five eight b. The first planet ever seen to transit, nineteen ninety-nine. A gas giant one point four times as wide as Jupiter, circling its star in only three point five days. It blocks about one point five percent of its star’s light: one of the deepest, easiest dips to see. It is so hot, over one thousand degrees Celsius, that gas is escaping from its atmosphere into a comet-like tail. Hot Jupiters are rare, but they were found first because they give big, frequent signals. Big and close equals deep dips that come often.

astronomy/kepler-laws.7691af8a379c: Kepler’s second law. Equal areas in equal times. The line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, also published in sixteen oh nine. So a planet moves fastest at perihelion, closest, and slowest at aphelion, farthest. Earth moves about thirty point three kilometers per second in early January and twenty-nine point three kilometers per second in early July. Halley’s Comet races past the Sun at about fifty-five kilometers per second but crawls at under one kilometer per second far beyond Neptune. Newton explained why: gravity pulls straight toward the Sun, so it can speed a planet up or slow it down but never change its “spin” around the Sun, angular momentum stays the same. Close equals short, fat wedge, fast. Far equals long, thin wedge, slow. Same area. Equal areas does not mean equal distances. Near perihelion the planet covers a much longer stretch of its orbit in the same time.
astronomy/kepler-laws.82b459fe53a1: Kepler’s first law. Orbits are ellipses, with the Sun at one focus. Published in sixteen oh nine in Kepler’s book Astronomia Nova, “New Astronomy”. The clue was Mars: Tycho Brahe’s measurements disagreed with a circular orbit by eight arcminutes, about a quarter of the Moon’s width. Kepler trusted the data and gave up circles. Eccentricity e measures how stretched an ellipse is: zero is a circle; close to one is a long, thin oval. Earth’s e is only zero point zero one seven, so its distance from the Sun only changes from about one hundred forty-seven to one hundred fifty-two million kilometers. Ellipse equals two pins and a loop of string. The Sun is one pin. Seasons are NOT caused by Earth getting closer to the Sun: Earth is closest in early January, during northern winter. Seasons come from Earth’s tilt.
astronomy/kepler-laws.d48d47e7a9eb: Kepler’s third law. T squared equals a cubed, years and AU. Published in sixteen nineteen in Harmonices Mundi, “The Harmony of the World”. T is the orbital period in years; a is the semi-major axis, half the long axis, the “average” distance, in AU. For every planet, T squared is about a cubed. Example: Jupiter, a equals five point two AU: a cubed equals one hundred forty-one, so T equals the square root of one hundred forty-one, about eleven point nine years. Newton showed the full rule: T squared equals four pi squared a cubed divided by G M, where M is the mass of the central body. Measure a moon’s orbit and you can weigh its planet! Farther out, slower AND a longer path, a much longer year. The law uses a, the average distance, semi-major axis, not the starting distance. Launch from the same spot at different speeds and you get different a and different T.
astronomy/kepler-laws.315793af06d0: Hohmann transfer. The fuel-saving road between two orbits. Described by German engineer Walter Hohmann in nineteen twenty-five, decades before any spacecraft flew. The transfer orbit is an ellipse with perihelion at Earth’s orbit, one AU, and aphelion at Mars’s orbit, one point five two AU, so a equals one point two six AU. By Kepler’s third law its full period is one point two six to the power of one point five, about one point four two years; the probe flies half of it: about two hundred fifty-nine days, or eight point five months. Real missions often spend a bit more fuel to arrive sooner: Perseverance took about two hundred three days, launched July thirtieth, twenty twenty, landed February eighteenth, twenty twenty-one. Speed up at Earth, coast half an ellipse, speed up again at Mars. You don’t aim at where Mars is when you launch. You aim at where Mars WILL BE about eight point five months later.
astronomy/kepler-laws.074c46d78ab1: Newton’s cannon. Orbit equals falling around the planet. Just above Earth’s surface, a circular orbit needs about seven point nine kilometers per second, about seventeen thousand seven hundred miles per hour. Higher up, less speed is needed because gravity is weaker there. Escape speed is the square root of two — about one point four one — times the circular speed: about eleven point two kilometers per second from the surface. The International Space Station flies about four hundred twenty kilometers up at about seven point six six kilometers per second and goes around Earth in about ninety-three minutes. Newton drew this thought experiment in a book published in seventeen twenty-eight, just after his death; the law of gravity itself appeared in his Principia, sixteen eighty-seven. Slow, falls. Seven point nine kilometers per second, circle. Faster, ellipse. Eleven point two kilometers per second, gone for good. There is plenty of gravity at the space station’s height: about eighty-nine percent of what you feel on the ground. Astronauts float because they are falling together with the station.
astronomy/kepler-laws.e33e9c34dbf0: Launch windows. Every twenty-six months, Mars is in the right place. Earth laps Mars about once every seven hundred eighty days, about twenty-six months. This is called the synodic period. A Hohmann launch needs Mars about forty-four degrees ahead of Earth. That lines up for only a few weeks each synodic period. In July twenty twenty, three Mars missions launched within eleven days: the UAE’s Hope, China’s Tianwen one and NASA’s Perseverance. Miss the window and you wait about two more years, which is why mission teams work around the clock before a launch. Twenty-six months: two years and two months between chances. Mars is not closest to Earth on launch day. The probe launches months before the two planets are closest, and arrives months after.

astronomy/rocketry.96446fe0ec1e: The gravity turn. Up first, then sideways. Rockets go straight up for the first few seconds to clear the tower and the thickest air. Then they tip a few degrees east, and gravity slowly bends the path over, so the rocket does not have to steer hard. Climbing straight up too long wastes fuel fighting gravity, “gravity loss”. Turning too early drags the rocket sideways through thick air, “drag loss”. Launching east from Florida adds about zero point four kilometers per second from Earth’s spin. Near the equator you get about zero point four six kilometers per second. A gentle nudge, then let gravity steer. Rockets do not go “up to space and then stop”. Without sideways speed they fall straight back down.
astronomy/rocketry.73a407e62f72: The rocket equation. Delta v equals exhaust velocity times the natural log of the quantity m zero divided by m sub f. Written down by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in nineteen oh three. Delta v is the total change in speed a rocket can make. It depends only on exhaust speed and the mass ratio: full mass m zero divided by empty mass m sub f. Reaching low Earth orbit needs about nine point four kilometers per second of delta v, seven point eight kilometers per second of orbital speed plus about one point five kilometers per second lost to gravity and drag. With exhaust velocity equals three kilometers per second, getting nine point four kilometers per second from one stage would need m zero divided by m sub f about twenty-three: the rocket would have to be about ninety-six percent fuel. That is why real rockets use stages. More fuel helps less and less: the mass ratio sits inside a logarithm. Delta v is not the top speed you will see. Gravity and drag eat part of it on the way up.
astronomy/rocketry.8916954c6faa: Staging. Throw away what you no longer need. When a stage runs out of fuel, it drops off with its empty tanks and engines. The rest of the rocket no longer has to carry that dead weight. Saturn five had three stages; Falcon nine and Long March five have two, plus side boosters on Long March five. Engines on upper stages are designed for vacuum: hydrogen engines like the R L one zero reach exhaust speeds of about four point five kilometers per second. Falcon nine first stages now fly back and land so they can be reused; some boosters have flown more than twenty times. Staging equals a relay race: each runner hands on a lighter rocket. Stages are not dropped because they are “used up” like a battery. They are dropped because empty tanks are heavy and useless.
astronomy/rocketry.29d1461ceb2b: What “orbit” means. Fast enough sideways to keep missing Earth. Space officially starts at about one hundred kilometers, the Kármán line. Reaching it takes about one point four kilometers per second straight up, or just a few minutes of flight. Staying in space is the hard part: at two hundred kilometers you need about seven point eight kilometers per second sideways, roughly twenty-three times the speed of sound at sea level. A suborbital flight, like a quick hop to one hundred kilometers and back, needs only a small fraction of the energy of an orbital flight. In orbit the engines switch off. Nothing slows you down, so you keep falling around Earth. Space equals one hundred kilometers up. Orbit equals seven point eight kilometers per second sideways. Reaching space is not the same as reaching orbit. The first needs height; the second needs enormous sideways speed.
astronomy/rocketry.581f3341d535: Thrust equals mass flow rate times exhaust velocity. How much mass, how fast. Thrust, in newtons, equals mass thrown out per second, kilograms per second, times exhaust speed, meters per second. Double either one and the thrust doubles. Engineers like high exhaust speed best, because it gives more push from each kilogram of fuel. One F one engine of the Saturn five burned about two point six tonnes of propellant every second, with an exhaust speed of about two point six kilometers per second: about six point eight million newtons. To lift off, the thrust must be bigger than the rocket’s weight. Thrust divided by weight at liftoff is usually about one point two to one point five. Thrust equals how much times how fast. A bigger flame does not always mean a better engine. Exhaust speed, not flame size, decides how far each kilogram of fuel can take you.
astronomy/rocketry.6b2b5bf5cbd1: Action and reaction. Newton’s third law makes rockets go. When the rocket pushes gas backward, the gas pushes the rocket forward with a force of exactly the same size. A rocket does not push against the air or the ground. It works even better in the vacuum of space, where no air gets in the way of the exhaust. In nineteen twenty a New York Times editorial mocked Robert Goddard for claiming rockets could work in a vacuum. In nineteen sixty-nine, as Apollo eleven flew to the Moon, the paper printed a correction. A garden hose kicks back in your hands for the same reason: water pushed one way pushes you the other way. Push gas back, gas pushes you forward. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Rockets do not need air to push on. The flame is not pushing the ground; the rocket is pushing its own exhaust.

astronomy/planets-moons.045feb7a6492: Ganymede. Moon of Jupiter. The largest moon in the solar system: wider than the planet Mercury, but with only about half of Mercury’s mass. The only moon known to make its own magnetic field, which even gives it auroras. A salty ocean is probably buried deep under its ice. ESA’s JUICE spacecraft is due to orbit it in twenty thirty-four. Ganymede equals the giant moon. Bigger than Mercury does not make Ganymede a planet: it orbits Jupiter, so it is a moon.
astronomy/planets-moons.8815d11b6951: Jupiter. Gas giant. It has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined; about one thousand three hundred Earths would fit inside. There is no solid surface: deep down, hydrogen is squeezed until it acts like a liquid metal, making a giant magnetic field. NASA’s Juno spacecraft has orbited Jupiter since twenty sixteen and found clusters of huge cyclones around both poles. Jupiter: biggest planet, shortest day, under ten hours. Jupiter is not a “failed star”: it would need about eighty times more mass to start nuclear fusion.
astronomy/planets-moons.e57ca87ac815: Enceladus. Moon of Saturn. Only five hundred four kilometers wide, about as wide as Arizona. Geysers from cracks at its south pole, “tiger stripes”, spray icy water into space, feeding one of Saturn’s rings. Cassini flew through the spray and found salt, organic molecules and hydrogen gas: signs of warm vents on the floor of a hidden ocean. Enceladus: tiny moon, giant geysers. Small does not mean frozen solid: tidal heating keeps Enceladus active inside.
astronomy/planets-moons.4f827ef708b8: Uranus. Ice giant. Tipped over ninety-eight degrees, so each pole gets about forty-two years of sunlight and then forty-two years of darkness. It has the coldest atmosphere of any planet: as low as minus two hundred twenty-four degrees Celsius. Only one spacecraft has ever visited: Voyager two, in January nineteen eighty-six. Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side. Neptune is farther away, but Uranus has the coldest air.
astronomy/planets-moons.a043d0edebbb: Saturn. Gas giant. It is less dense than water, zero point six nine grams per cubic centimeter. The main rings span about two hundred eighty thousand kilometers but are mostly only about ten meters thick, made of chunks of water ice. Cassini orbited Saturn from two thousand four to twenty seventeen and ended by diving into Saturn so it could never crash onto a moon that might hold life. Saturn: rings and the most known moons, two hundred ninety-three. The rings do not vanish: about every fifteen years we see them edge-on, and they are so thin they almost disappear.
astronomy/planets-moons.87e35133f749: Venus. Rocky planet. The air pressure at the surface is ninety-two times Earth’s, like being nine hundred meters, three thousand feet, under the ocean. It spins backward, so the Sun rises in the west. Sunrise to sunrise takes one hundred seventeen Earth days. Its carbon dioxide blanket traps heat, a runaway greenhouse effect: about four hundred sixty-five degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. Venus: Earth-sized, but a greenhouse oven. Venus is not hot because it is close to the Sun; it is hot because its C O two air traps heat.
astronomy/planets-moons.9540baa7f83e: Io. Moon of Jupiter. The most volcanic world we know: more than four hundred active volcanoes. Jupiter’s tides squeeze and stretch Io as it orbits; the resonance with Europa and Ganymede keeps its orbit slightly oval, so the squeezing never stops and heats its insides. Sulfur and sulfur dioxide frost paint it yellow, orange, red and white. Io: innermost big moon, a world of volcanoes. Io’s heat does not come from the Sun; it comes from tidal squeezing by Jupiter.
astronomy/planets-moons.14f675e6f2fe: Neptune. Ice giant. The fastest winds in the solar system: about two thousand kilometers per hour, one thousand two hundred miles per hour. In eighteen forty-six it was found by math: astronomers predicted where it must be from the way it tugged on Uranus. Its largest moon, Triton, orbits backward and has geysers of nitrogen gas. Neptune: one year equals one hundred sixty-five Earth years. Neptune is blue because methane gas absorbs red light, not because it is covered in water.
astronomy/planets-moons.9079a710a759: Europa. Moon of Jupiter. Under an ice shell probably fifteen to twenty-five kilometers thick is a salty ocean holding about twice as much water as all of Earth’s oceans. Reddish-brown cracks and ridges criss-cross its smooth, young icy surface. NASA’s Europa Clipper launched in October twenty twenty-four and is due to reach Jupiter in twenty thirty to study whether Europa could support life. Europa: an ocean world wearing an ice shell. Europa is far too cold for liquid water on top; its ocean stays liquid because tidal heating warms it from inside.
astronomy/planets-moons.e8010d1945d3: Pluto. Dwarf planet. A dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt, smaller than our Moon. In twenty fifteen New Horizons found a heart-shaped plain of frozen nitrogen and mountains made of water ice. Its moon Charon is half as wide as Pluto; the two orbit a point in the space between them. One Pluto year equals two hundred forty-eight Earth years. Pluto was not reclassified just for being small: it has not cleared its orbit of other objects.
astronomy/planets-moons.996846436fd1: Europa. Under an ice shell probably fifteen to twenty-five kilometers thick is a salty ocean holding about twice as much water as all of Earth’s oceans. Reddish-brown cracks and ridges criss-cross its smooth, young icy surface. NASA’s Europa Clipper launched in October twenty twenty-four and is due to reach Jupiter in twenty thirty to study whether Europa could support life. Europa: an ocean world wearing an ice shell.
astronomy/planets-moons.e07e65565897: GALILEAN MOONS. Four big moons. Galileo found them in January sixteen ten with a small telescope. Seeing moons circle another planet showed that not everything orbits Earth. Io, Europa and Ganymede tug on each other in a one to two to four rhythm, an orbital resonance. Those regular tugs keep their orbits slightly oval, so Jupiter’s tides flex them and heat their insides: volcanoes on Io, an ocean under Europa’s ice. You can see all four with ordinary binoculars as tiny dots next to Jupiter. MEMORY HINT. Order outward: “I Eat Green Cheese” equals Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto. Common mix-up: A resonance does not mean the moons line up all together: in fact Io, Europa and Ganymede can never all be on the same side of Jupiter at once.
astronomy/planets-moons.94b0bb1d5587: Jupiter. It has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined; about one thousand three hundred Earths would fit inside. There is no solid surface: deep down, hydrogen is squeezed until it acts like a liquid metal, making a giant magnetic field. NASA’s Juno spacecraft has orbited Jupiter since twenty sixteen and found clusters of huge cyclones around both poles. Jupiter: biggest planet, shortest day, under ten hours.
astronomy/planets-moons.014266e969b3: Callisto. The most heavily cratered object in the solar system: its surface is about four billion years old. It orbits every sixteen point seven days and is NOT part of the one to two to four resonance, so tides barely heat it. It is far enough from Jupiter’s radiation that it may be a future base for astronauts. Callisto: the quiet, cratered outsider.
astronomy/planets-moons.10f0afaaee8f: The Moon. Moon of Earth. It probably formed when a Mars-sized body crashed into the young Earth about four point five billion years ago. Craters near its south pole that never see sunlight hold water ice, a target for NASA’s Artemis astronauts. It drifts about three point eight centimeters, one point five inches, farther from Earth every year. Moon gravity about one sixth of Earth’s. The Moon does spin: exactly once per orbit, which is why we always see the same face.
astronomy/planets-moons.c3469bfbe32b: Io. The most volcanic world we know: more than four hundred active volcanoes. Jupiter’s tides squeeze and stretch Io as it orbits; the resonance with Europa and Ganymede keeps its orbit slightly oval, so the squeezing never stops and heats its insides. Sulfur and sulfur dioxide frost paint it yellow, orange, red and white. Io: innermost big moon, a world of volcanoes.
astronomy/planets-moons.be378b2a75a1: Ganymede. The largest moon in the solar system: wider than the planet Mercury, but with only about half of Mercury’s mass. The only moon known to make its own magnetic field, which even gives it auroras. A salty ocean is probably buried deep under its ice. ESA’s JUICE spacecraft is due to orbit it in twenty thirty-four. Ganymede equals the giant moon.
astronomy/planets-moons.13da444e314c: Titan. Moon of Saturn. The only moon with a thick atmosphere; its orange haze hides the surface. Liquid methane and ethane fall as rain and fill rivers, lakes and seas; Ligeia Mare is bigger than Lake Superior. The Huygens probe landed there in two thousand five. NASA’s Dragonfly drone is planned to launch in twenty twenty-eight and fly between sites on Titan. Titan: a moon with weather, methane rain. Titan’s lakes are not water: at minus one hundred seventy-nine degrees Celsius water is as hard as rock. They are liquid methane and ethane.
astronomy/planets-moons.63e4c9f62841: Earth. Rocky planet. The densest planet in the solar system, five point five times the density of water. The only world known to have liquid water on its surface right now, and life. Its magnetic field and ozone layer shield life from the solar wind and ultraviolet light. Earth is the measuring stick: one gee, one day, one year, one AU. Earth is not a perfect ball: it bulges a little at the equator, twelve thousand seven hundred fifty-six kilometers across versus twelve thousand seven hundred fourteen kilometers pole to pole.
astronomy/planets-moons.530b43c8be7d: Mercury. Rocky planet. From one sunrise to the next takes one hundred seventy-six Earth days: that is two whole Mercury years. Even here, water ice hides in craters near the poles that never see sunlight. Its iron core fills about eighty-five percent of its radius, so for its size it is very dense. Mercury: smallest planet, shortest year, eighty-eight days. Closest to the Sun is not hottest on average: Venus is hotter.
astronomy/planets-moons.c3cdb451f903: Common mix-up: Heavy things do not fall faster. In nineteen seventy-one Apollo fifteen astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the airless Moon: they hit the ground together.
astronomy/planets-moons.95857155931b: Mars. Rocky planet. Olympus Mons is about twenty-two kilometers high, two point five times Mount Everest; the canyon Valles Marineris is about four thousand kilometers long, as wide as the USA. The air is so thin that liquid water quickly boils away or freezes, but ice fills its polar caps and lies under the ground. Since twenty twenty-one the Perseverance rover has been collecting rock samples in Jezero Crater, an ancient lake bed. A Mars day, a “sol”, is twenty-four hours forty minutes, almost like ours. Mars is red because of rust, iron oxide, in its dust, not because it is hot.

astronomy/small-bodies.c4f223d04b54: Halley’s Comet. Edmond Halley predicted its return for seventeen fifty-eight using Newton’s laws, the first comet known to come back. In nineteen eighty-six the European spacecraft Giotto flew within six hundred kilometers of its nucleus: a dark, potato-shaped lump about fifteen kilometers long. Its orbit is tilted and goes around backward compared with the planets. Dust it left behind causes two meteor showers: the Eta Aquariids, May, and the Orionids, October. Comets live on long, stretched ellipses: fast near the Sun, slow far away.
astronomy/small-bodies.32f854ca25f4: Common mix-up: The Kuiper Belt is not the edge of the solar system: the Oort Cloud lies about fifty to two thousand times farther out.
astronomy/small-bodies.d2e8c44ca274: Oort Cloud, schematic. A giant, roughly spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the whole solar system. We infer it from the orbits of comets that fall in from every direction. A passing star or the pull of the Milky Way can nudge an Oort Cloud object inward, and it becomes a long-period comet like Hale-Bopp. Its outer edge may reach a third of the way to the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, two hundred sixty-eight thousand astronomical units. Short trips, less than two hundred years, Kuiper Belt comets; very long trips, Oort Cloud comets.
astronomy/small-bodies.e6b1edbdb472: Common mix-up: Pluto is not the most massive dwarf planet: Eris has about twenty-seven percent more mass, though Pluto is slightly wider.
astronomy/small-bodies.91353631d262: Pluto and friends. Pluto’s stretched orbit sometimes brings it closer to the Sun than Neptune, last time nineteen seventy-nine to nineteen ninety-nine, but the two can never collide: Pluto goes around twice for every three Neptune orbits. New Horizons, twenty fifteen, found glaciers of nitrogen ice, mountains of water ice and a blue hazy sky. Eris, discovered in two thousand five, is almost exactly Pluto’s size; finding it led astronomers to create the “dwarf planet” category in two thousand six. Dwarf planet: round, orbits the Sun, but has not cleared its neighbourhood.
astronomy/small-bodies.abe37d7bc416: Kuiper Belt. A doughnut-shaped belt like the asteroid belt, but about twenty times wider and made mostly of ice. On January first, twenty nineteen, New Horizons flew past Arrokoth, a thirty-six kilometer “snowman” made of two lumps that gently stuck together: an untouched building block of planets. Many comets that return in less than two hundred years start out here or in the nearby scattered disk. Asteroid belt equals rock, close in. Kuiper Belt equals ice, far out.
astronomy/small-bodies.d88bce138070: Near-Earth asteroids. These asteroids were nudged out of the belt and now cross or come near Earth’s orbit. Osiris Rex collected a sample from Bennu and dropped it in the Utah desert in September twenty twenty-three. Asteroid Apophis, about three hundred forty meters, will pass Earth on April thirteenth, twenty twenty-nine, closer than some satellites, and will be visible without a telescope. It will not hit us. Planetary defense equals find them early, track them, and, if needed, push them.
astronomy/small-bodies.18b3d0be401d: Voyager one. The most distant human-made object. In August twenty twelve, at about one hundred twenty-one astronomical units, it crossed the heliopause into interstellar space. Around late twenty twenty-six it is about one light-day from Earth: a radio command takes about twenty-four hours to reach it. Even so, it would take about three hundred years to reach the inner edge of the Oort Cloud and perhaps thirty thousand years to pass through it. One light-day about one hundred seventy-three astronomical units.
astronomy/small-bodies.d6748601e57c: Main asteroid belt. Asteroids are rocky or metal leftovers from when the planets formed four point six billion years ago. Jupiter’s gravity kept them from ever building a planet. Vesta, five hundred twenty-five kilometers, has a giant crater at its south pole; pieces blasted out of it have landed on Earth as meteorites. NASA’s Psyche spacecraft is on its way to a metal-rich asteroid, arriving in twenty twenty-nine. The belt sits between Mars and Jupiter: “rocks between the red and the giant”.
astronomy/small-bodies.82bf160058af: Jupiter Trojans. Two swarms share Jupiter’s orbit, one leading and one trailing, held at balance points where the Sun’s and Jupiter’s gravity work together, Lagrange points L four and L five. They are dark, reddish and may be “fossils” left over from the outer solar system. NASA’s Lucy spacecraft, launched in twenty twenty-one, will fly past several Trojans starting in twenty twenty-seven. Trojans travel with Jupiter like two groups of runners sixty degrees ahead and behind.
astronomy/small-bodies.a2668ecc5d24: SMALL BODIES. The solar system’s leftovers. Besides eight planets, the Sun is circled by millions of asteroids, comets and dwarf planets. Where they live tells us what they are made of. Asteroids: rock and metal, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter, warm enough that ice could not survive there. Comets: ice and dust, from the cold Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud. Meteoroids: small pieces broken off asteroids and comets. MEMORY HINT. Rocks inside, ice outside: the “frost line”, about three astronomical units, split the young solar system. Common mix-up: A “shooting star” is not a star: it is a grain of dust burning up about one hundred kilometers above your head.

astronomy/big-bang.134cbe4dfaea: Protons and neutrons form. After about ten millionths of a second it is “cool” enough, a few trillion degrees, for quarks to clump in threes into protons and neutrons.
astronomy/big-bang.74d05261aa46: Life on Earth. At least three point five billion years ago, maybe earlier, simple single-celled microbes live in Earth’s oceans. Animals come much later: the first dinosaurs only two hundred thirty million years ago.
astronomy/big-bang.32f22c95fdef: Galaxy G N z one one. Found by Hubble, twenty sixteen, studied by Webb. We see it as it was about four hundred million years after the Big Bang. Its light set out almost nine billion years before the Sun and Earth formed.
astronomy/big-bang.209a63e73dc5: The first nuclei, three to twenty minutes. For about twenty minutes the whole universe is a nuclear fusion reactor. Protons and neutrons fuse into helium nuclei, plus a little deuterium and lithium. Result: about seventy-five percent hydrogen and twenty-five percent helium by mass, exactly what we measure in the oldest gas and stars.
astronomy/big-bang.4fb080f8a4a2: The Sun. One hundred fifty million kilometers away. Sunlight takes eight minutes twenty seconds to reach Earth. If the Sun suddenly vanished, we would keep seeing it, and orbiting it, for over eight minutes.
astronomy/big-bang.e3f5020975e6: Dark energy takes over. As galaxies spread apart, matter’s gravity weakens and dark energy wins. The expansion, which had been slowing down, starts to speed up. Astronomers discovered this in nineteen ninety-eight using Type one A supernovae.
astronomy/big-bang.34c3ffcd6bba: First atoms: the CMB is released, three hundred eighty thousand years. Until now light kept bouncing off free electrons, like headlights in fog. At about three thousand kelvins electrons join nuclei to make the first atoms, the fog clears, and light travels freely. That light is the cosmic microwave background we still detect today.
astronomy/big-bang.55bf96a9ff2d: Cosmic noon. About three billion years in, galaxies make new stars roughly ten times faster than today. Galaxies collide and merge, and giant black holes in their centers blaze as quasars.
astronomy/big-bang.ba7a1fb1cc04: The first galaxies. The James Webb Space Telescope has found galaxies seen just two hundred ninety million years after the Big Bang, such as JADES G S z one four dash zero, already surprisingly bright. Small galaxies merge to build bigger ones.
astronomy/big-bang.8b9e07670701: M eight seven in the Virgo Cluster. A giant elliptical galaxy, fifty-three million light-years away. Its light left about twelve million years after an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs. Its central black hole was the first one ever photographed, twenty nineteen.
astronomy/big-bang.02d95fad96f1: The cosmic microwave background. The farthest light there is. Released three hundred eighty thousand years after the Big Bang, from every direction at once. Before this the universe was an opaque fog: no light from earlier can reach us.
astronomy/big-bang.2ee47d4ef27f: Galaxy JADES G S z one four dash zero. Found by JWST in twenty twenty-four; the distance record holder until twenty twenty-five. We see it only about two hundred ninety million years after the Big Bang. Its light was stretched so much that it arrives as infrared, which is why Webb was built to see infrared.
astronomy/big-bang.54da1d11ed13: Cosmic dawn: the first stars. Around one hundred to two hundred million years, gas in dark-matter clumps collapses into the first stars: huge, hot and blue, made only of hydrogen and helium. When they explode they make the first carbon, oxygen and iron, and their light starts to clear the hydrogen fog, reionization.
astronomy/big-bang.59744e804583: Today: thirteen point eight billion years. Space between the galaxies is just two point seven degrees above absolute zero, and the expansion is speeding up. If all of cosmic history were squeezed into one year, modern humans would appear in the last eleven minutes of December thirty-first.
astronomy/big-bang.25a9c2290cf2: Inflation. In far less than a trillionth of a trillionth of a second, a tiny patch of space balloons by an enormous factor, at least ten to the power of twenty-six times. Tiny quantum jitters get stretched into the seeds of every future galaxy. This is the least certain part of the story: strong clues, not yet proven.
astronomy/big-bang.6e09acab295f: Quasar three C two seven three. The first quasar identified, nineteen sixty-three. A galaxy whose central black hole is swallowing gas so fast that it outshines its whole galaxy hundreds of times over. When its light set out, life on Earth was still only single-celled.
astronomy/big-bang.f8bf3be71b4d: Center of the Milky Way. About twenty-six thousand light-years away. Its light left during the last ice age, when mammoths roamed North America. We can’t see it with our eyes, dust blocks it, but infrared and radio telescopes can.
astronomy/big-bang.6b84616c2fab: Proxima Centauri. The nearest star, four point two four light-years away. The light you would see tonight left it about four years ago. A message sent there by radio today would arrive around twenty thirty-one, and a reply would come back around twenty thirty-five.
astronomy/big-bang.300ca5245f26: The Moon. Three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away. Moonlight, really reflected sunlight, takes one point three seconds to reach you. So the Moon you see is the Moon of about one heartbeat ago.
astronomy/big-bang.fc44a5ec7dd8: The Sun and Earth form. Four point six billion years ago, a cloud of gas enriched by generations of earlier stars collapses into the Sun and a disk that becomes the planets. The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were made inside those earlier stars.
astronomy/big-bang.bdef9f019206: Andromeda Galaxy. The farthest thing you can see with your eyes alone. Two point five million light-years away: the light entering your eye left when the first members of our human genus, Homo, were appearing in Africa. On a dark autumn night you can see it as a faint smudge in the constellation Andromeda.

astronomy/three-body.6d2f92860411: Each star feels the pull of the others. We choose model units for distance, mass and time so the gravity constant G has a value of one. The clock counts model seconds. Velocity Verlet updates the motion every zero point zero zero zero five model seconds. In B and C, a softening length, epsilon equals zero point zero zero eight, keeps acceleration finite during close passes. In A and the two-star preset, "epsilon equals zero" gives ordinary Newtonian gravity. The line in the sky view marks the distance r between stars one and two. Move the time slider to see how much acceleration star two alone gives star one. The mass of star two is m sub two.
astronomy/three-body.61407b981606: In an ideal, isolated pair, two bound stars that do not collide keep tracing ellipses around their shared center of mass. A circle is a special ellipse. Try the two-star control and see whether the stars retrace their paths. As the three stars move, all their pulls change. There’s no simple general formula for their motion from arbitrary starting conditions. Henri Poincaré’s work revealed how complicated the motion can get. In chaos, 混沌, tiny differences at the start can grow into big differences later, even under the same rules.
astronomy/three-body.28689b34d742: Three equal-mass stars chase each other around the same loop. Watch them take turns at the crossing. Chenciner and Montgomery published a proof of this orbit in two thousand.
astronomy/three-body.493d7d5b53ca: Alpha Centauri is the closest star system to ours. Stars A and B form a close pair, and Proxima Centauri orbits much farther out. Preset B shows this arrangement with a smaller difference in orbit sizes so you can see both at once. Picture two massive bodies circling each other. There are five special positions where a much lighter spacecraft can move along with them and keep the same position relative to both. In this circular-orbit model, those positions are called Lagrange points. Measurements of temperature and wind always have some uncertainty. Like the zero point zero zero one shift in the butterfly experiment, tiny starting differences can grow as the atmosphere moves. Research puts the limit for day-to-day forecasts in midlatitudes, where much of the United States lies, at about two weeks. Liu Cixin’s The Three-Body Problem is a science-fiction novel for older readers. It won the twenty fifteen Hugo Award for Best Novel. Its Trisolaran world has three suns. During Stable Eras, days and nights follow a pattern. During Chaotic Eras, sunrise and temperature become unpredictable.

chemistry/atoms.262fcdf767dc: Neutron. Neutral, zero, particle in the nucleus. Charge: zero. Mass: about one atomic mass unit, a tiny bit heavier than a proton. Neutrons help hold the nucleus together. Without them, the positive protons would push each other apart. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes.
chemistry/atoms.3fb186243859: Nucleus. The tiny, heavy center of the atom. Made of protons and neutrons packed tightly together. Holds more than ninety-nine point nine percent of the atom’s mass, but only a tiny part of its volume. If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea at the center. The nucleus has a positive charge because of its protons.
chemistry/atoms.43dd1909ec37: Electron. Negative, minus one, particle around the nucleus. Charge: minus one. Mass: about one over one thousand eight hundred thirty-six of a proton, so it barely counts toward the mass. Electrons are arranged in shells, energy levels, around the nucleus. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. Electrons in the outermost shell, valence electrons, take part in chemical reactions.
chemistry/atoms.da8361adfee6: Atomic number. equals number of protons. Every element has its own atomic number: H is one, C is six, O is eight. The periodic table is arranged in order of atomic number. In a neutral atom, it also equals the number of electrons.
chemistry/atoms.de81465ff36c: Mass number. equals protons plus neutrons. Electrons are so light that we don’t count them. Neutrons equals mass number minus atomic number. Example: carbon fourteen has fourteen minus six equals eight neutrons. The number after an element’s name, carbon twelve, is its mass number.
chemistry/atoms.3e30816245c1: Common mix-up: The third shell can actually hold eighteen electrons, but for the first twenty elements it holds eight before the fourth shell starts.
chemistry/atoms.7396bc35da59: Schrödinger and others. Electron-cloud, quantum, model. Electrons do not follow exact paths. We can only say where they are likely to be: a fuzzy electron cloud. In nineteen thirty-two Chadwick discovered the neutron, completing today’s picture. Experiments showed that electrons behave like waves as well as particles.
chemistry/atoms.428f222e73d5: Electron shell. Energy levels where electrons are found. For elements one to twenty: shell one holds up to two electrons, shell two up to eight, shell three up to eight, the two-eight-eight rule. Electrons fill the inner shells first, then move outward. Atoms with a full outer shell, like helium, neon and argon, are very stable and unreactive.
chemistry/atoms.e232784686e1: Proton. Positive, plus one, particle in the nucleus. Charge: plus one. Mass: about one atomic mass unit, A M U. The number of protons is the atomic number, and it decides WHICH element the atom is. Add or remove one proton and the atom becomes a different element. Try it!
chemistry/atoms.7e493199129c: Electron cloud. Today’s model: where electrons are LIKELY to be. Scientists cannot know exactly where an electron is at any moment, only where it is likely to be. Where the cloud is thicker, the electron is more likely to be found. This quantum, cloud, model came from scientists such as Schrödinger in the nineteen twenties.
chemistry/atoms.02b72df6be1b: Ion. An atom with unequal protons and electrons. Lose electrons, more protons than electrons, positive ion, cation, for example, sodium ion. Gain electrons, more electrons than protons, negative ion, anion, for example, chloride ion. Table salt is made of sodium and chloride ions held together.
chemistry/atoms.5c7b59fd782b: Isotope. Same protons, different neutrons. Carbon twelve, carbon thirteen and carbon fourteen are all carbon: each has six protons. Some isotopes are radioactive, unstable. Carbon fourteen is used to find the age of things that were once alive, up to about fifty thousand years old. Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium, zero neutrons, deuterium, one neutron, and tritium, two neutrons.

chemistry/periodic-table.e9f11ccb880c: Neodymium. Lanthanides. atomic number sixty. Elements fifty-seven to seventy-one, shown in the first row at the bottom. Used in strong magnets, phone screens and lasers.
chemistry/periodic-table.45af92da53d8: Promethium. Lanthanides. atomic number sixty-one. Elements fifty-seven to seventy-one, shown in the first row at the bottom. Used in strong magnets, phone screens and lasers.
chemistry/periodic-table.065f18323579: Zirconium. Transition metals. atomic number forty. Groups three to twelve, the middle block. Hard, strong, shiny metals that conduct heat and electricity well: iron, copper, gold, silver.
chemistry/periodic-table.8fc27bb92df6: Bismuth. Post-transition metals. atomic number eighty-three. Softer metals to the right of the transition metals, such as aluminum, tin and lead.
chemistry/periodic-table.8aa364fffb3a: Chromium. Transition metals. atomic number twenty-four. Groups three to twelve, the middle block. Hard, strong, shiny metals that conduct heat and electricity well: iron, copper, gold, silver.
chemistry/periodic-table.de71369a8403: Radium. Alkaline earth metals. atomic number eighty-eight. Group two. Shiny, fairly reactive metals with two valence electrons. Calcium builds your bones and teeth.
chemistry/periodic-table.6db0b442d863: Thallium. Post-transition metals. atomic number eighty-one. Softer metals to the right of the transition metals, such as aluminum, tin and lead.
chemistry/periodic-table.bbbec2ae6f27: Sulfur. Other nonmetals. atomic number sixteen. A yellow solid that smells when it forms compounds, like rotten eggs, hydrogen sulfide.
chemistry/periodic-table.1f504bd7bd78: Platinum. Transition metals. atomic number seventy-eight. A precious metal used in jewelry and in car catalytic converters.
chemistry/periodic-table.c83ad37348bb: Antimony. Metalloids. atomic number fifty-one. Along the staircase line. They have properties of both metals and nonmetals. Silicon is a semiconductor used in computer chips.
chemistry/periodic-table.cbdd6baa709e: Noble gases. Group eighteen. Their outer shells are full, so they almost never react. Neon glows in signs; helium fills balloons.
chemistry/periodic-table.c4615e1ecd96: Phosphorus. Other nonmetals. atomic number fifteen. Found in your bones, teeth and DNA. Matches use red phosphorus.
chemistry/periodic-table.3d0ab7355c12: Sodium. Alkali metals. atomic number eleven. A soft metal you can cut with a knife. It fizzes and can burst into flame in water. With chlorine it makes table salt.
chemistry/periodic-table.0b316caa6305: Dubnium. Transition metals. atomic number one hundred five. Groups three to twelve, the middle block. Hard, strong, shiny metals that conduct heat and electricity well: iron, copper, gold, silver.
chemistry/periodic-table.9b198c8f0385: Potassium. Alkali metals. atomic number nineteen. Bananas are rich in potassium. Your nerves and muscles need it to work.
chemistry/periodic-table.a6195bd0ab7b: Osmium. Transition metals. atomic number seventy-six. The densest natural element: a fist-sized chunk would weigh about as much as a small dog.
chemistry/periodic-table.85265d018d5d: Meitnerium. Transition metals. atomic number one hundred nine. Groups three to twelve, the middle block. Hard, strong, shiny metals that conduct heat and electricity well: iron, copper, gold, silver.
chemistry/periodic-table.68963140f96f: Common mix-up: Hydrogen is in group one but is NOT an alkali metal.
chemistry/periodic-table.4bb99ddba650: Rubidium. Alkali metals. atomic number thirty-seven. Group one, except hydrogen. Soft, shiny metals with one valence electron. So reactive with water that they are stored in oil.
chemistry/periodic-table.6b3813b9d0ce: Arsenic. Metalloids. atomic number thirty-three. Along the staircase line. They have properties of both metals and nonmetals. Silicon is a semiconductor used in computer chips.
chemistry/periodic-table.f3feef538383: Bohrium. Transition metals. atomic number one hundred seven. Groups three to twelve, the middle block. Hard, strong, shiny metals that conduct heat and electricity well: iron, copper, gold, silver.
chemistry/periodic-table.c7f44a047e3b: Cobalt. Transition metals. atomic number twenty-seven. Groups three to twelve, the middle block. Hard, strong, shiny metals that conduct heat and electricity well: iron, copper, gold, silver.
chemistry/periodic-table.ff735957d4da: Oganesson. Noble gases. atomic number one hundred eighteen. The heaviest element known, one hundred eighteen. Only a handful of atoms have ever been made, each lasting less than a thousandth of a second.

chemistry/states-of-matter.5ce71fb892e4: Melting. Solid, liquid, heat is absorbed. Ice melts at zero degrees Celsius. This is its melting point. While melting, the temperature stays at zero degrees Celsius until all the ice has melted. The energy breaks the lattice apart. Melting one gram of ice takes three hundred thirty-four joules of energy.
chemistry/states-of-matter.25fe7eb4beca: Sublimation. Solid, gas, skipping the liquid, heat is absorbed. Particles at the surface of a solid escape straight into the gas. Dry ice, solid carbon dioxide, sublimates at minus seventy-eight degrees Celsius: it never becomes a puddle. Snow can slowly disappear on cold, sunny, dry days without melting.
chemistry/states-of-matter.7651119ecf3b: Temperature. How fast the particles move on average. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy, motion energy, of the particles. Hotter equals particles move faster. Colder equals particles move slower. At absolute zero, minus two hundred seventy-three degrees Celsius, particle motion is at its lowest possible level.
chemistry/states-of-matter.1d4bcef7d5f2: Freezing. Liquid, solid, heat is released. Water freezes at zero degrees Celsius, the same temperature at which ice melts. Particles slow down until attractions lock them into a lattice. Freezing releases heat. Farmers spray water on fruit trees on frosty nights so the freezing water protects the fruit.
chemistry/states-of-matter.ebd6e8aa3f6f: Water molecule, H two O. The tiny particle that makes up water. All matter is made of tiny particles, atoms or molecules, that are always moving. Each water molecule is one oxygen atom, red, joined to two hydrogen atoms, white. Ice, liquid water and steam are made of exactly the same molecules. Only their spacing and motion change.
chemistry/states-of-matter.6b49bc7ed8d2: Common mix-up: Changing state is a physical change. No new substance forms: H two O stays H two O.
chemistry/states-of-matter.bba515ba816c: Vaporization, boiling and evaporation. Liquid, gas, heat is absorbed. Evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature. That is how puddles dry up. Boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point: one hundred degrees Celsius for water at sea level. Boiling one gram of water takes two thousand two hundred sixty joules, almost seven times more than melting it!

chemistry/elements-compounds.18613adceb15: Common mix-up: N H three is not flat. Nitrogen also has a pair of unshared electrons on top, which pushes the three H atoms down into a pyramid.
chemistry/elements-compounds.ebfa33402985: Table salt, sodium chloride. Compound, pure substance. Ions stacked in a crystal. Sodium ions and chloride ions attract each other and stack in a repeating cube pattern called a crystal lattice. There are no separate N a C l molecules. The formula gives the ratio: one N a for every one C l. Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, and chlorine is a poisonous gas. Bonded together, they make the salt you eat! Salt grains are little cubes because the ions stack like cubes.
chemistry/elements-compounds.b7c9cb9ad6a3: Carbon dioxide. Compound, pure substance. A straight-line molecule. One carbon atom sits between two oxygen atoms in a straight line, one hundred eighty degrees. Each C equals O double bondlink is a double bond. You breathe out C O two; plants take it in for photosynthesis. “di” means two: carbon DIoxide has two oxygens.
chemistry/elements-compounds.408b75c54594: Common mix-up: Sand is mostly the compound S i O two and iron is an element, but mixing them does not make a new compound.
chemistry/elements-compounds.99da708bd1c7: Common mix-up: The four belongs only to H, not to C. C H four does not have four carbons.
chemistry/elements-compounds.c4a6b020cbc6: Sand and iron filings. Heterogeneous mixture. You can see the parts. You can see the different parts: tan sand grains and gray iron bits. One spoonful might have more iron than another. The mixture is not the same everywhere. A magnet pulls out the iron because iron is magnetic and sand is not. Mixtures can be separated by physical means. Heterogeneous equals “different” parts you can see or pick out.
chemistry/elements-compounds.729aa574553f: Oxygen gas. Element, pure substance. Only one kind of atom. Made only of oxygen atoms, so it is an element, a pure substance. Two oxygen atoms share electrons in a double bond to form one O two molecule. About twenty-one percent of the air is O two. You need it to breathe, and fires need it to burn. Element equals only ONE kind of atom, even if the atoms are joined in pairs.
chemistry/elements-compounds.2f3562e6a19c: Iron. Element, pure substance. A metal made of single atoms. Iron is an element: every atom in it has twenty-six protons. Metal atoms are not grouped into molecules. They pack together in a repeating crystal. Iron is magnetic, which helps us pull it out of mixtures. Symbols: first letter CAPITAL, second letter lowercase. F e comes from the Latin word “ferrum”.
chemistry/elements-compounds.31b77b4067a8: Common mix-up: O two is a molecule, but it is NOT a compound. A compound needs two or more DIFFERENT elements.
chemistry/elements-compounds.36be04f9576e: Ammonia. Compound, pure substance. A pyramid-shaped molecule. One nitrogen atom bonds to three hydrogen atoms. The molecule is a short pyramid with N at the top, H N H about one hundred seven degrees. Ammonia is used to make fertilizers and is found in some cleaners. It has a strong smell. N H three: one Nitrogen, three Hydrogens.
chemistry/elements-compounds.6eb9c3f09f7a: Air. Homogeneous mixture. A mixture of gases. Air is about seventy-eight percent nitrogen, N two, twenty-one percent oxygen, O two, almost one percent argon, A r, plus a tiny bit of C O two, about zero point zero four percent, and water vapor. The gases are mixed evenly but are NOT bonded to each other. Each keeps its own properties. The amounts can change: a crowded room has more C O two, and air near the ocean has more water vapor. Mixture equals substances mixed but not bonded; the “recipe” can change.
chemistry/elements-compounds.d72334c81049: Methane. Compound, pure substance. A tetrahedron-shaped molecule. Methane is the main part of natural gas, used for cooking and heating. The four hydrogen atoms point to the corners of a tetrahedron, one hundred nine point five degrees apart, as far from each other as possible. Carbon usually forms four bonds. That is why it can build so many different molecules. No subscript means one: C H four equals one C plus four H equals five atoms.
chemistry/elements-compounds.cdb4b5844075: Common mix-up: Air contains O two and N two molecules, but air is not a compound. There is no single formula for air.
chemistry/elements-compounds.1f609ad9f51d: Common mix-up: C O, carbon monoxide, “mono” equals one, is a different, poisonous gas. One oxygen atom makes a big difference.
chemistry/elements-compounds.aa558d7439db: Water. Compound, pure substance. Two hydrogen and one oxygen, bonded. Two elements, hydrogen and oxygen, are chemically bonded, so water is a compound. The molecule is bent: the H O H angle is about one hundred four point five degrees. Every water molecule has the same two to one ratio of H to O. A compound always has a fixed ratio. Water is totally different from its elements: H two burns and O two helps fires, but water puts fires out! A subscript counts the atom just before it: H two O equals H double bond, H, O.
chemistry/elements-compounds.b4db0a0fee68: Common mix-up: H two O two, hydrogen peroxide, is a different compound. Change a subscript and you change the substance.

chemistry/changes.7cf6a6ca848f: Baking soda and vinegar. Is it a physical or a chemical change? Make a prediction, then run the experiment.

chemistry/reactions.ae251210f84c: Common mix-up: You need two O two, not one: the products contain four O atoms, two in C O two plus one in each H two O.
chemistry/reactions.2ba34c04cbef: Methane burns. Combustion. Methane, natural gas, burns in oxygen. This is the flame on a gas stove. The products are carbon dioxide and water vapor, both invisible gases. Count: one C, four H and four O on each side. Mass: eighty atomic mass units, eighty atomic mass units. In an open kitchen the gases drift away, so it looks like the fuel just disappears. Burn something made of C and H in O two and you always get C O two and H two O.
chemistry/reactions.5a4984868b89: Hydrogen burns. Synthesis, combustion. First the H single-bond H and O double-bond O must break. Then the atoms regroup: each O atom bonds to two H atoms, making two H two O. Count: four H and two O before, four H and two O after. Mass: thirty-six atomic mass units, thirty-six atomic mass units. This reaction releases lots of energy. It powers some rockets and fuel-cell cars. Atoms are like LEGO bricks: take the model apart and build something new. Same bricks, new shape.
chemistry/reactions.1906bccc613b: Making ammonia. Synthesis. Nitrogen and hydrogen join to make ammonia, which is used to make fertilizer. The strong triple bond in N two is hard to break, so factories use heat, high pressure and a catalyst. Count: two N and six H on each side. Mass: thirty-four atomic mass units, thirty-four atomic mass units. Four molecules become two molecules, but the number of atoms stays eight. Molecules can change in number. Atoms can’t.
chemistry/reactions.0f1e3b3d9d19: Common mix-up: The two in front of H two O is a coefficient, two molecules. Writing H two O two instead would make a different substance: hydrogen peroxide!
chemistry/reactions.383759796717: Splitting water. Decomposition. Electricity splits water into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas: the reverse of hydrogen burning. Two water molecules react to form two H two and one O two. Count: four H and two O on each side. Mass: thirty-six atomic mass units, thirty-six atomic mass units. One reactant breaking into simpler substances is called decomposition. Decomposition: one thing, two or more things.

chemistry/solutions.14cfa57e52ba: Solution. A mixture that is the same all through. Solution equals solute and solvent. It is a homogeneous mixture: the same everywhere. Solutions are transparent, see-through, even when colored, like blue copper sulfate solution. The solute never settles out of a solution, no matter how long it sits. Mass is conserved: mass of solution equals mass of solute plus mass of solvent.
chemistry/solutions.4d7ae81b49ec: Common mix-up: Dissolving is not melting! Melting needs heat to turn a solid into a liquid; dissolving is when solute particles spread out between solvent particles. The sugar’s mass doesn’t vanish: one hundred grams of water plus twenty grams of sugar equals one hundred twenty grams of sugar water.
chemistry/solutions.a76bef3c9066: Solubility. The most that can dissolve. Solubility is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in one hundred grams of solvent at a given temperature. At twenty degrees Celsius, one hundred grams of water dissolves about two hundred four grams of sugar but only about thirty-six grams of table salt. Solubility is a physical property — it can help identify a substance. For most solids, solubility increases as temperature rises.
chemistry/solutions.5e90cdd48613: Particle size. Smaller pieces dissolve faster. Crushing a solid into powder gives it far more surface area touching the solvent. Granulated sugar dissolves faster than a sugar cube, but the same total mass dissolves in the end. Cutting one cube into eight smaller cubes doubles the surface area.
chemistry/solutions.a61b609da4ad: Common mix-up: Divide by the mass of the solution, solute plus solvent, not just the water.
chemistry/solutions.67d4bfc17069: Temperature. Speeds dissolving and changes solubility. Hot water particles move faster, so they hit the solid more often and with more energy. For most solids, a higher temperature means a higher solubility: K N O three goes from about thirty-two grams, twenty degrees Celsius, to one hundred sixty-nine grams, eighty degrees Celsius. Salt barely changes: about thirty-six grams at twenty degrees Celsius and thirty-eight grams at eighty degrees Celsius. Gases are the opposite: they dissolve less in warm water.
chemistry/solutions.399d11f40f3d: Concentration. How much solute is in the solution. Concentration tells how much solute is dissolved in a certain amount of solution. Mass percent equals mass of solute divided by mass of solution times one hundred percent. Example: twenty grams of sugar in one hundred grams of water, twenty divided by one hundred twenty, about sixteen point seven percent. Concentrated equals lots of solute; dilute equals little solute. Adding water dilutes a solution. With a colored solute such as copper sulfate, a more concentrated solution looks darker. Try it!

chemistry/acids-bases.4f6d10b54274: Antacid, milk of magnesia. pH ten point five. Basic. Antacids are bases that neutralize extra stomach acid to relieve heartburn. Stomach acid, hydrochloric acid, has a pH of about one point five to three point five.
chemistry/acids-bases.064778f8cb5f: Seawater. pH eight point one. Basic. Seawater is slightly basic, about pH eight point one. As the ocean absorbs C O two from the air its pH slowly drops, ocean acidification, which harms shells and coral.
chemistry/acids-bases.8d562653caf9: The pH scale. Measures acidity from zero to fourteen. pH runs from zero, most acidic, through seven, neutral, to fourteen, most basic. pH tells how many hydrogen ions are in a solution: the more hydrogen ions, the lower the pH. Each step is a times ten change: pH three is ten times more acidic than pH four and one hundred times more acidic than pH five.
chemistry/acids-bases.e184573b3a70: Household ammonia. pH eleven point six. Very basic. A base used in glass cleaners. Never mix ammonia with bleach — it makes a toxic gas!
chemistry/acids-bases.c336a86b3864: Battery acid. pH zero point eight. Very acidic. Car batteries contain sulfuric acid, H two S O four. It is corrosive: it can burn skin and eat holes in clothing.
chemistry/acids-bases.e0ff77f9b800: Neutralization. Acid and base react to form salt and water. When an acid and a base react, hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions join to make water: hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions react to form H two O. The other ions form a salt. Example: H C l and N a O H react to form N a C l and H two O. If equal amounts react, the solution ends up neutral, pH about seven. Everyday uses: antacids for heartburn, soapy water on itchy insect bites, formic acid, and slaked lime to fix acidic soil.
chemistry/acids-bases.bbf80f09ec63: Base. pH above seven. Bases release hydroxide ions in water. They taste bitter and feel slippery, like soap. Bases turn red litmus blue and turn phenolphthalein pink.
chemistry/acids-bases.9cc1cbcbd5e9: Milk. pH six point six. Acidic. Milk is almost neutral, just slightly acidic. When milk goes sour, bacteria make lactic acid and the pH drops.
chemistry/acids-bases.7240d67993f4: Tomato. pH four point three. Acidic. Tomatoes are mildly acidic — that’s why tomato sauce tastes tangy.
chemistry/acids-bases.336f94954620: Lemon juice. pH two point two. Very acidic. Citric acid gives lemons their sour taste. A sour taste is a property of acids.
chemistry/acids-bases.f916e5576f44: Neutral. pH equals seven. A neutral solution is neither acidic nor basic: pH seven. Pure water is neutral because it has equal amounts of hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions. Salt water and sugar water are neutral too.
chemistry/acids-bases.42c0e979639a: Black coffee. pH five. Acidic. Coffee is only weakly acidic. Normal rain is also slightly acidic, about pH five point six, because carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in it.
chemistry/acids-bases.5c8859da73e1: Drain cleaner. pH thirteen point eight. Very basic. Contains sodium hydroxide, lye, one of the strongest common bases. It dissolves hair and grease in pipes — and can badly burn skin and eyes.
chemistry/acids-bases.f982345e658d: Pure water. pH seven. Neutral. Pure, distilled, water is neutral: pH seven at twenty-five degrees Celsius. It has equal amounts of hydrogen and hydroxide ions. Tap water is usually between pH six point five and eight point five.
chemistry/acids-bases.44b77ef48edc: Acid. pH below seven. Acids release hydrogen ions in water. They taste sour, lemons, vinegar — but never taste lab chemicals! Acids turn blue litmus paper red and purple litmus solution red. Many acids react with metals such as zinc to make hydrogen gas.
chemistry/acids-bases.c7640a907e4f: Vinegar. pH two point nine. Very acidic. Vinegar is about five percent acetic acid in water. It is used for cooking, pickling and removing hard-water scale.
chemistry/acids-bases.bce4997f28f6: Orange juice. pH three point five. Acidic. Contains citric acid and ascorbic acid, vitamin C. Lemon juice, pH two point two, is about twenty times more acidic.
chemistry/acids-bases.be71458c666b: Bleach. pH twelve point six. Very basic. Bleach, sodium hypochlorite solution, is strongly basic and a powerful disinfectant. Bases feel slippery because they react with the oils on your skin.

chemistry/density.8e31f1330d02: Aluminum cube. Two point seven grams per cubic centimeter. It is denser than every liquid, so it sinks all the way to the bottom.
chemistry/density.f7bac8a71dea: Ping-pong ball. Zero point zero eight grams per cubic centimeter. It floats on top of the Rubbing alcohol, with about ten percent of it under the surface.
chemistry/density.3dc3309c4bf1: Your object. Two point seven grams per cubic centimeter. It is denser than every liquid, so it sinks all the way to the bottom.
chemistry/density.91d3582c100b: Your object. One point two grams per cubic centimeter. It sinks through Rubbing alcohol, Vegetable oil, Water, Dish soap, all less dense than one point two, and floats on top of the Corn syrup, one point three three.
chemistry/density.0982f2485dd5: Vegetable oil. Zero point nine two grams per cubic centimeter. Vegetable oil is about zero point nine two grams per cubic centimeter. Oil and water do not mix, and the less dense oil floats on top. That’s why an oil spill spreads out over the surface of the sea.
chemistry/density.687b9a20ab81: Corn syrup, dyed purple. One point three three grams per cubic centimeter. Corn syrup is sugar, glucose, dissolved in water. One hundred milliliters has a mass of about one hundred thirty-three grams. It is a little less dense than honey, so it floats on top of the honey.
chemistry/density.912783d7c291: Dish soap. One point zero six grams per cubic centimeter. Dish soap is about one point zero six grams per cubic centimeter — just a little denser than water. One hundred milliliters has a mass of about one hundred six grams. It must be poured slowly, or it mixes with the water layer.
chemistry/density.86b5c2200a8c: Cork. Zero point two four grams per cubic centimeter. It floats on top of the Rubbing alcohol, with about thirty percent of it under the surface.
chemistry/density.34edf3f9a9f3: Water, dyed blue. One gram per cubic centimeter. Water has a density of one point zero zero grams per cubic centimeter, zero point nine nine eight at room temperature. So one milliliter of water has a mass of one gram — an easy number to remember! Objects less dense than one gram per cubic centimeter float in water; denser objects sink.
chemistry/density.d569a0a25870: Honey. One point four two grams per cubic centimeter. Honey is mostly sugar with a little water — lots of mass packed into each cubic centimeter. One hundred milliliters of honey has a mass of about one hundred forty-two grams. It is also very viscous, thick, so objects sink through it slowly.
chemistry/density.1be604382f30: Density. Mass per unit volume. Density equals mass divided by volume, D equals m divided by V. Units: grams per cubic centimeter, the same as grams per milliliter. It tells how tightly matter is packed — how much mass is squeezed into each cubic centimeter. Density is a physical property: each pure substance has its own density, which helps identify it. Cutting an object in half halves both the mass and the volume, so its density stays the same.
chemistry/density.dfce6c098e7d: Pine wood block. Zero point five grams per cubic centimeter. It floats on top of the Rubbing alcohol, with about sixty-three percent of it under the surface.
chemistry/density.2e26f61c8eb8: Steel nut. Seven point eight seven grams per cubic centimeter. It is denser than every liquid, so it sinks all the way to the bottom.
chemistry/density.3cf7405f288e: Rubbing alcohol, dyed red. Zero point seven nine grams per cubic centimeter. Rubbing, isopropyl, alcohol is about zero point seven nine grams per cubic centimeter — the least dense liquid here. It would mix with water, but the oil layer keeps them apart. One hundred milliliters has a mass of only about seventy-nine grams.

chemistry/oxygen-air.921cc2a3b8e6: About twenty-one milliliters of every one hundred milliliters of dry air is oxygen, using the same temperature and pressure for both volumes. Air is a mixture. Dry-air figures leave out water vapor, which varies in real air.
chemistry/oxygen-air.ac3cb91652da: Red phosphorus, 红磷, reacts with oxygen to form phosphorus pentoxide. Tiny solid particles form white smoke.
chemistry/oxygen-air.dcf79a2e5696: The school equation represents the black product as magnetite, F e three O four. Which iron oxides actually form can depend on the conditions. At room temperature and pressure, oxygen is a colorless, odorless gas. It is slightly denser than air and only slightly soluble in water. Oxygen supports combustion. In these reactions it reacts with the material that burns.
chemistry/oxygen-air.7e5489a56ccb: Fine particles, P M two point five, can reach deep into the lungs. Sulfur dioxide, S O two, nitrogen dioxide, N O two, and ground-level ozone, O three, are examples of gaseous pollutants. Use the Air Quality Index, AQI, to check local air quality.
chemistry/oxygen-air.eb3dc4af790a: Most of this last one percent is argon, a noble gas. It also includes carbon dioxide and other trace gases. Air is a mixture. Dry-air figures leave out water vapor, which varies in real air.

chemistry/carbon.c433617a9b50: Burning fossil fuels transfers carbon from long-term underground stores to the air as C O two.
chemistry/carbon.56c95b392c8e: C O poisoning happens when C O binds to hemoglobin, the protein in blood that carries oxygen. This interferes with oxygen delivery and can cause headaches, dizziness and even death. If a C O alarm sounds or you suspect poisoning, get to fresh air outside immediately and call emergency services from there, nine one one in the US.
chemistry/carbon.878db50a741c: The surface absorbs sunlight and emits infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases such as C O two absorb and re-emit some infrared radiation. The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm. Added C O two strengthens it. Arrows show direction and relative change.
chemistry/carbon.8b650e92fdc9: C O two can also leave surface water and return to the air. Ocean-air exchange goes both ways.
chemistry/carbon.42f933d9287d: Why is the C O two heavier than the methane used? The oxygen in C O two comes from O two in the air. Count the water as well when comparing total masses.
chemistry/carbon.895a9a0d65b4: Organisms release C O two during cellular respiration. Decomposers also return carbon to the air as they break down dead plants and animals.
chemistry/carbon.afdff4744e0a: Some C O two from the air dissolves in surface seawater. Some of that dissolved C O two reacts with water to form carbonic acid. The carbon can also enter other dissolved forms or become part of living things.
chemistry/carbon.46f265f4182b: Limestone or marble reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid without heating. At the same temperature and pressure, C O two is denser than air. Feed it near the bottom of an upright jar so it displaces air upward. Some C O two dissolves in water, so collection over water loses some gas.
chemistry/carbon.e74425d063f4: A C sixty molecule is a hollow cage with a carbon atom at each corner. Its twelve pentagons and twenty hexagons form a pattern like the panels of a soccer ball. Sixty atoms in one molecule. Each carbon has three bonded neighbors.
chemistry/carbon.6124381cfa59: Plants take C O two from the air during photosynthesis and use its carbon to make sugars.
chemistry/carbon.266a035afd3e: The same two carbon atoms get enough oxygen to form two C O two molecules. The equation shows the simplest ratio.

chemistry/metals.0650fc81d762: Many metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides. The metal and the reaction conditions determine what you observe. Fine iron wire burns with sparks in oxygen and can form black F e three O four. In damp air, iron rusts slowly.
chemistry/metals.5a2e981df288: Most metals are shiny and conduct heat and electricity well. They can usually be pressed into sheets, malleability, or drawn into wires, ductility. Hardness, density, and melting point vary. Mercury is liquid at room temperature. An alloy, héjīn, 合金, is a metallic material made by combining a metal with other elements. Many alloys are harder than their main pure metal. Many also start melting at a lower temperature than that metal. Copper is common in wires because it conducts electricity well and is easy to draw into wire. Brass is a copper-zinc alloy. Its combination of workability and corrosion resistance makes it useful for fittings such as taps.
chemistry/metals.aa3cde02fbfa: Most metals are shiny and conduct heat and electricity well. They can usually be pressed into sheets, malleability, or drawn into wires, ductility.
